transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. Could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yes, thank you for seeing me. Um, well, it's been a long time coming, I guess, but what finally scared me into actually making the appointment and coming in today is work. I work in video production—I shoot and edit, mostly TV and film stuff, which I love, I really do—and it’s a job where you really, really can’t afford to mess up the little things, you know? The workflow is so specific and everyone relies on the person before them. 

But lately, I just... I keep making these incredibly dumb technical mistakes. And it’s so frustrating because I *know* better. I have my degree in this, I’ve been doing it for years, but I’ll do things like label the camera cards completely wrong after a long shoot, which is an absolute nightmare for the data wranglers and assistant editors. Or I'll be in the editing bay going through notes and just completely miss a timecode note from the director. Just skip right over it. 

The worst part, the thing that really made me panic last week and pick up the phone to call your office, was when I exported a final client cut and sent it off, and it had the wrong lower-third graphic on the screen. And the crazy thing is, I checked it! I swear I checked it before I hit export, I sat there and watched it down, but somehow my eyes just didn't register that it was the wrong name on the graphic. It’s like my brain just skips over the details, and honestly, it’s terrifying because in this industry, your reputation is everything, and I could lose my job over this kind of stuff if I keep looking this sloppy. I just don't understand why I can't catch these things when I'm literally looking right at them...
Over the past couple of weeks, have you been feeling down, sad, or noticing that you've lost interest or pleasure in things you normally enjoy?

No, no, not at all. I mean, I get incredibly frustrated with myself, obviously, because of the mistakes I just mentioned, but I wouldn't say I feel sad or down. And I definitely haven't lost interest in things. I still absolutely love my job, which is exactly why this is all so stressful for me! 

Like, just this past weekend, I was out shooting some B-roll for a friend's indie documentary—just a little side passion project about local community gardens—and I was completely into it. I spent hours just geeking out over the natural lighting and getting these really beautiful macro shots of the bees and the soil, trying out a new lens I just rented, and I was having the time of my life. I still love doing all that. The passion is one hundred percent still there. 

And I still love my hobbies outside of work, too. I'm always wanting to go out, go hiking with my dog, see friends, go to trivia nights... I have plenty of energy and excitement for all the things I usually enjoy. It's really just the panic of, you know, dropping the ball at my actual paying job that's bothering me. But as far as feeling depressed or losing my spark for things? No, definitely not. I still want to do everything, I just want to be able to do it without making these careless errors that make me look incompetent, you know? So, no, not sad. Just really, really annoyed with myself.

Thinking back to your school years or childhood, did you have similar issues with careless mistakes, losing focus, or forgetting details back then, or is this pattern something that's only shown up recently as an adult?

Oh, wow. Um, okay, so... yeah. Actually, yes. Now that you say that, it really isn't new at all. I mean, it's funny you bring up school because I was just talking to my mom about this the other day, and she was reminding me about how—well, I guess I've always been kind of like this, just maybe in different ways? 

Like, I remember even back in elementary school, like third or fourth grade, my teachers were constantly having to move my desk. I was never, ever in my seat. I'd be up sharpening my pencil for the fifth time, or going to look at the class pet, or just wandering over to see what someone else was doing. And I was always the kid blurting out answers before the teacher even finished the question. Like, I just couldn't hold it in. I'd know the answer, or think I knew the answer, and my hand wouldn't even go up, the words would just fly out of my mouth. 

And I was always bothering my classmates, too. Not meaning to! Just, you know, I'd lean over and start talking to whoever was next to me about whatever random thought popped into my head, completely interrupting them while they were trying to work. And the thing is, I wouldn't even realize I was doing it until the teacher would call my name and tell me to turn around or sit down. It was like my body and my mouth were moving faster than my brain could catch up to tell them to stop. 

So my desk was always getting moved to the front row, right by the teacher's desk, or sometimes even isolated in the back of the room so I wouldn't distract anyone else. And my report cards... oh my gosh, every single one of them said "talks too much," "needs to stay in her seat," "rushes through work and makes careless errors." So, yeah, the careless mistakes and the... I guess the impulsivity of it all? That's definitely been there since I was a little kid. It just looks different now that I'm 38 and working in video production instead of sitting in Mrs. Gable's fourth-grade math class, you know? But the underlying feeling of just... moving too fast and missing things? Yeah, that's always been there.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports current, functionally impairing inattentive symptoms (careless errors, missing details, failure to fully process visual/textual information) causing occupational risk, in the absence of any depressive or anxiety symptoms that could better explain the inattentiveness. Crucially, she confirms a childhood history (documented via report cards and parental recollection) of clear inattentive (careless mistakes, distractibility), hyperactive (unable to stay seated, excessive movement), and impulsive (blurting answers, interrupting others) symptoms beginning by elementary school age, establishing childhood onset. The persistence of both inattentive and impulsive/hyperactive traits from childhood into adulthood, with continued functional impairment, supports a diagnosis of ADHD, combined presentation (ICD-10 F90.0), rather than a purely inattentive or unspecified subtype.
